title_original: The Great Kelly Clarkson Wind-Up Bird Feud, Explained
excerpt_original: Plus, a confounding list of culture's Free Thinkers, 'The Bowery: Devil’s Mile,' and other art world matters.

A Personal Note Re: Kelly Clarkson’s Feud With a Brooklyn Magic Shop…

OK, here’s a very silly but very big story: “Miss Independent” singer Kelly Clarkson is in a furious internet dispute with tiny Brooklyn magic shop the Art of Play over whether or not its staff was rude to her when she inquired about buying a certain singing bird sculpture. Seriously, look it up. Huge story . I’m here to say: I’m team Art of Play all the way. It sells incredible puzzles sourced from around the world, and I saw the best magic show of my life—by the incomparable David Williamson —in the hidden theater behind the bookshelf in the back. While I was there, I also happened to ask about the magic wind-up bird sculpture, which the owners show off before each performance. It’s by an artist named Bliss Kolb from Seattle. Being from Seattle myself and having a dad who loves clocks and other wind-up gizmos, I also, like Clarkson, wanted more details, and I will say the staff seemed mildly cagey. But I simply interpreted this as them maintaining an air of mystery. The bird in question is like the mascot for the store! And the entire wonder of the store is that it feels full of secrets!

blocks.text: A Random List of Culture’s ‘Free Thinkers’…

For some reason, for its 40th birthday, the Independent has dropped the “Independent’s Free Thinkers List,” featuring “people who have exhibited free thinking” during the paper’s lifetime. The 40 chosen Free Thinkers include artists Ai Weiwei (“changing the possibilities of politically engaged contemporary art“) and Tracey Emin (“helped make confession, vulnerability and autobiography legitimate subjects for contemporary art”). These picks do not exactly symbolize “radical free-thinking”; they are pretty familiar. The rest of the list’s grab bag includes the likes of Virgil Abloh , Richard Dawkins , Deng Xiaoping , Elon Musk , Shonda Rhimes , Margaret Thatcher , and Donald J. Trump . What a head-scratcher.
A Second Opinion on Mark Fisher…

The late theorist Mark Fisher , author of Capitalist Realism (2009), remains one of the major theory references in an art writing world that has largely replaced theory with attitude. Writer and researcher Rômulo Moraes has a scathing, attitude- and theory-filled dissent at his blog Ear Vortex . The one-line summary is this: Fisher was “a producer of false urgencies and chewed-up thought processes lifted and resized from the better work of others.” I happen to agree that Fisher’s cultural pessimism has outlived its sell-by date, reprocessed into the dull work of a commentator like W. David Marx in Blank Space (2025). To Moraes’s credit, the bulk of his essay is devoted to proposing thinkers he sees as better than Fisher.

An Anniversary-of-Note for the Art-Pod-Sphere…

The OG art podcast, Chicago-based weekly Bad at Sports , celebrated 999 episodes at the beginning of this month, with a big live onstage conversation at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago featuring New York mag’s critic, Jerry Saltz . That’s just one shy of 1,000 episodes! An accomplishment worth celebrating! I’ve been on B@S twice, and both times (episode # 767 , in 2021, and # 912 , last year), the chatty informal style let us get both weirder and more personal than almost anywhere else. The Saltz ep, which goes up online and on Lumpen Radio , will come out later in 2026. Congrats!
Something Not to Miss…

“ The Bowery: Devil’s Mile ” is an unexpected crowd-pleaser at the New Museum , not to be lost in the furor over Arthur Jafa , which opened at the same time (odd habit, that—almost guaranteeing things get lost in the mix). Surveying the long, long history of the Bowery as a creative site, the show serves as former New Museum director Lisa Phillips ’s final show, as if to put her legacy in context, and is co-curated by up-and-comer Thalia Stefaniuk . (At the press conference, Phillips affectionately compared their dynamic to the show Hacks ). Art highlights range from portraits of Bowery characters by Billy Sullivan and a suite of engaging sculptures by contemporary artist Brad Kahlhamer , whose studio is on the Bowery, to Jacob Riis ’s formative social documentary work How the Other Half Lives (1890) and Nan Goldin ’s incomparably moving The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1985). But—surprisingly or unsurprisingly—the copious well-chosen non-art artifacts pack just as much punch, fleshing out the New York neighborhood’s history as a site of creative experimentation in the fullest popular sense. A civic-minded, serious, and seriously delightful exhibition.
